group.title: Useful adjectives
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Sudden and unexpected, often in an unpleasant way.
examples: The meeting came to an {abrupt} end.
wrong: The change was abrupt because it took ten slow years.

words.meaning: Enough or good enough for a purpose.
examples: The room has {adequate} space for ten people.
wrong: The food was adequate, so half the guests went hungry.

words.meaning: Easy to see or understand.
examples: It soon became {apparent} that we were lost.
wrong: The answer was apparent, so nobody could see it.

words.meaning: Brave and willing to take risks.
examples: It was a {bold} decision to start her own company.
wrong: His bold plan was to avoid every risk.

words.meaning: Without a strong taste or anything interesting.
examples: The soup was {bland}, so I added salt and pepper.
wrong: The curry was bland and full of strong spices.

words.meaning: Quick and full of energy.
examples: We went for a {brisk} walk before breakfast.
wrong: We took a brisk walk, moving slowly and lazily.

words.meaning: Completely confused and without any order.
examples: The airport was {chaotic} after the strike.
wrong: The room was chaotic, with everything in perfect order.

words.meaning: Unkind, cruel or too severe.
examples: The coach’s {harsh} words upset the players.
wrong: His harsh comment was gentle and full of praise.

words.meaning: Large in size, amount or importance.
examples: The project cost a {considerable} amount of money.
wrong: He spent a considerable sum, only a few cents.

words.meaning: Always behaving or happening in the same way.
examples: She is a {consistent} player who rarely makes mistakes.
wrong: His work is consistent: great one day, terrible the next.

words.meaning: Extremely important, because other things depend on it.
examples: Sleep is {crucial} for good health.
wrong: This step is crucial, so you can skip it.

words.meaning: Having parts very close together; thick.
examples: We got lost in the {dense} forest.
wrong: The fog was dense, so we could see for miles.

words.meaning: Clearly different or easy to notice.
examples: There’s a {distinct} smell of smoke in here.
wrong: The two colors are distinct; you can’t tell them apart.

words.meaning: Allowed to do or receive something because you meet the rules.
examples: You’re {eligible} to vote when you turn eighteen.
wrong: He’s not old enough, so he’s eligible for the adult team.

words.meaning: Very strong, angry or violent.
examples: The two companies are in {fierce} competition.
wrong: The fierce dog lay gently and wagged its tail at everyone.

words.meaning: Easily broken or damaged.
examples: Be careful with that vase; it’s very {fragile}.
wrong: The glass is fragile, so you can drop it safely.

words.meaning: Real and true, not fake.
examples: Is this a {genuine} leather bag?
wrong: The painting is genuine; it’s a cheap copy.

words.meaning: Very busy and full of activity.
examples: It’s been a {hectic} week at work.
wrong: We had a hectic day, relaxing on the sofa.

words.meaning: Lower in quality or value than something else.
examples: The copy is {inferior} to the original.
wrong: This phone is inferior, so it’s the best on the market.

words.meaning: Complete and not damaged.
examples: The old castle walls are still {intact}.
wrong: The vase arrived intact, broken into ten pieces.

words.meaning: Very interested in something and eager to do it.
examples: He’s {keen} on photography.
wrong: She’s keen to join the club, so she refused to apply.

words.meaning: Allowed by law, or fair and reasonable.
examples: She had a {legitimate} reason for being late.
wrong: It’s a legitimate business that breaks every law.

words.meaning: Not as strict as expected when punishing someone.
examples: The judge was {lenient} because it was a first mistake.
wrong: The lenient teacher gave everyone the hardest punishment.

words.meaning: Used to say how small or unimportant something is.
examples: The shop is a {mere} five minutes away.
wrong: It’s a mere hundred miles, a very long journey.

words.meaning: Not well known, or hard to understand.
examples: He quoted an {obscure} poet nobody had heard of.
wrong: The obscure singer is famous all over the world.

words.meaning: Continuing for a long time, or not giving up easily.
examples: I have a {persistent} cough that won’t go away.
wrong: The persistent salesman left after one polite no.

words.meaning: Strong and not likely to break or fail.
examples: This laptop has a {robust} metal case.
wrong: The robust chair broke the first time I sat on it.

words.meaning: Stiff and not able to bend, or not willing to change.
examples: The school has very {rigid} rules.
wrong: His rigid plan changed every few minutes.

words.meaning: Not deep.
examples: The children played in the {shallow} end of the pool.
wrong: The lake is shallow, so the bottom is far beyond reach.

words.meaning: Rising or falling sharply, so hard to climb.
examples: The road up the hill is very {steep}.
wrong: The path was steep and completely flat.

words.meaning: Long, slow and boring.
examples: Filling in all these forms is {tedious}.
wrong: The tedious film was exciting from start to finish.

words.meaning: Very clear, bright and easy to imagine.
examples: I have {vivid} memories of my first day at school.
wrong: My memory of it is vivid; I can’t remember anything.

words.meaning: Easily hurt, harmed or attacked.
examples: Young children are {vulnerable} to colds in winter.
wrong: The castle was vulnerable, so no army could ever enter it.

words.meaning: Very tired, especially after long effort.
examples: The {weary} travelers finally reached the hotel.
wrong: She felt weary and full of fresh energy.

words.meaning: Making you feel uncomfortable or embarrassed.
examples: There was an {awkward} silence after his joke.
wrong: The meeting was awkward, and everyone felt totally at ease.

words.meaning: Very strange and unusual.
examples: It was a {bizarre} dream about talking fish.
wrong: Brushing your teeth is a bizarre habit nobody has.

words.meaning: Good enough or of an acceptable standard.
examples: Is there a {decent} restaurant near here?
wrong: The hotel was decent, so we left after five minutes in disgust.

words.meaning: Extremely large or great.
examples: The new stadium is {immense}.
wrong: The immense box fit easily in my pocket.

words.meaning: Exact and accurate in every detail.
examples: Can you give me the {precise} time of the delivery?
wrong: He gave precise directions: go somewhere over there.

words.meaning: Strong and solidly made.
examples: You’ll need {sturdy} boots for this hike.
wrong: The sturdy table wobbled and fell apart.
